speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: asked the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance what is the Government's response to Singapore's recent drop in ranking in the International Institute for Management Development's World Talent Ranking 2025, which assesses the three pillars of investment and development, appeal and readiness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: It provides a perspective of how Singapore is perceived vis-a-vis the other economies as a global talent hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Singapore's performance should also be seen in context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For example, demographic realities limit how much we can grow our workforce.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: As such, our slowing labour force growth in 2024 resulted in a fall in the related indicator.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This is a testament to our cost-effective public spending on education.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Singapore will continue to welcome talent who complement our own capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We will, at the same time, press on with our priority in developing our local workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Indeed, perception, sometimes, they say, is reality unless we clarify or correct them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I have two supplementary questions and based on the remarks that are made by the directors from IMD.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One is under the pillar of investments and development.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am baffled why the report cites that we have low education investment, when education is actually known to be one of the highest items in our Annual Budget.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And especially, I wonder if the report has considered factors, like the hefty investments that we have made in adults' continued training and education in SkillsFuture, and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And also, at the same time, a director from IMD mentioned that Singapore has done more than enough, despite the so-called "relatively low" education investment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second supplementary question pertains to the pillar of appeal.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The report also cited that, because organisations are relocating to relatively low-cost countries in, especially near our neighbouring countries, it claims that companies, therefore, could get a similar quality workforce for a much lower price in these countries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I would like to hear the Minister's comment on this, whether that is, indeed, true or is it just a comment on Singapore?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in 2016, for example, we were 15; then in 2017, 13; in 2018, 13.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, in 2024 it was second, and now it is 2025.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we have had a few ups and downs, but, overall, the trend has been upwards and we are still in the top 10.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the first point I want to make.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, the second point to make is how do they measure this competitiveness?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It assesses the 69 economies using the following three factors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, investment and development that evaluates the investment in and the development of homegrown talent; then it looks at appeal, which measures the ability to attract and retain overseas talent; and third, it looks at readiness, which assesses whether the existing talent pool meets current and future needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, let us look and see how we did on these three factors, which whilst addressing this, will also address the Member's supplementary question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the expenditure on education, actually, that is not very different from last year's report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that has not been much of a shift.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These indicators, the part on education as a percentage of GDP, have traditionally weighed down our rankings across the years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that seems to be because they look to see how much you put in.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Whereas for us, it is not only just how much we put in.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it does not seem to give enough weight to the value-for-money part.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And also, the indicator that is used in the IMD report on education investment is on public expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, given Singapore's relatively high GDP, the percentage figure will naturally appear lower compared to other countries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this does not mean that our actual investment in education is small.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore consistently allocates one of the largest portions of our Annual Budget to education, as the Member has pointed out, including substantial investments through initiatives, such as SkillsFuture.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, our total public expenditure on education per student, rather than as a percentage of GDP, remains relatively high.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the same IMD report, we were ranked 17th this year on this indicator, and our pupil-teacher ratio is still comparable to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) averages and to that of countries like, the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Korea and Japan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think these indicators do not fully capture the strength of our education system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our outcomes remain strong in education, as reflected in the international benchmarks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On this first factor, it is more the perception-based indicators on employee training and apprenticeships that pulled the ranking down.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second factor on appeal, on many of the traditional considerations, we remain largely the same.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is, for management, fair administration of justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The things that weighed us down on appeal were perception-based indicators on worker retention.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was a fall in executives' perception for indicators, such as worker motivation in companies; and secondly, a high cost of living.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That one did not move that much though; it was from 63rd to 65th.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore ranked 65th, which is comparable to other overall top performers, like Switzerland and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and ahead of Hong Kong.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And so, this indicator has traditionally weighed down our overall ranking over the years, but it is not a key factor pulling down the ranking in 2025.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our performance in the readiness factor was relatively steady, and for this one, it reflected our strong education system serving as a notable strength.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore ranked highly in PISA, as well as the proportion of science, technology, engineering or mathematics (STEM) graduates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the surveys also affirmed that our primary and secondary and university education meets the needs of the competitive economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the areas of decline, under readiness, was labour force growth, I addressed that earlier, and perception indicators on availability of skilled labour and specific skillsets and expertise.
